rituals.hook: Catch the instant an unchosen thought begins.
rituals.play: Rest on one neutral point. When a thought appears by itself, catch only its first instant before following it.
rituals.twist: Classify only its form—word, image, memory, plan, sensation—then release.
rituals.reveal: You notice an arrival before it becomes a complete thought.
rituals.mindBend: A thought can arrive before choice enters the room.
rituals.safety: Use only one ordinary thought. If forced mental blankness appears, stop and look at a physical object nearby.

rituals.hook: Catch the instant a thought stops being present.

rituals.mindBend: Thoughts also have natural endings.
rituals.safety: Stay with a brief thought sample. If the exercise shifts into forced mental blankness, end there; allow your thoughts to move normally again.

rituals.hook: Allow thought one but deny it a sequel.
rituals.rule: The first thought is permitted in full.

rituals.reveal: The original thought ends without becoming a chain.
rituals.mindBend: The first thought is not the loop.
rituals.safety: Keep this to everyday mental content. When compulsive thought monitoring appears, step out and move back to everyday activity.

rituals.hook: Force multiple arrivals into a one-at-a-time queue.
rituals.rule: Only one item can occupy the front slot.
rituals.play: When several thoughts compete, imagine numbered tickets. Process only the lowest number for three beats; all others wait silently.
rituals.twist: After three beats, move the front ticket to the back without solving it.
rituals.reveal: Competition becomes an orderly sequence rather than a pile-up.
rituals.mindBend: Maybe overload is not too many thoughts.
rituals.safety: Choose everyday mental content. When greater thought preoccupation appears, end the round; do something simple and concrete.

rituals.safety: Use everyday mental content. When forced mental blankness becomes noticeable, end it there and switch to a routine task.

rituals.play: View the present thought written on a paper page; turn the page over to reveal a blank next page.
rituals.twist: Keep the old page behind you.
rituals.reveal: The thought becomes located on a completed page.
rituals.mindBend: A thought can remain represented while being turned away from view.
rituals.safety: Make this a brief exercise with low-charge mental text for one pass. When obsessive wording checks develop, stop at that point and leave the wording alone.

rituals.safety: Use low-charge mental text for one pass. When more threatening text develops, end the round; look at real text nearby.

rituals.mindBend: The brain supplies a crisp boundary where no triangle line was drawn.
rituals.safety: Keep the round within low-intensity content. If visual unreality or strain increases, step away from the exercise and find one reliable visual anchor.

rituals.safety: For one pass, use a short look at thinking. If detachment from ordinary activity appears, stop the round; return to a concrete task.

rituals.safety: Make this a brief exercise with stable external cues. When the exercise shifts into dizziness or disorientation, stop at that point and orient outward to something stable.

rituals.hook: Repair the thought with exactly one move.
rituals.rule: Only one mental piece may change; everything else is locked.
rituals.play: Identify the smallest assumption or relationship that, if altered once, would make the conclusion fit the known facts better. Move only that one piece.
rituals.twist: If you need a second repair, restore the first and try a different single move instead.
rituals.reveal: A rigid conclusion may depend on one badly placed assumption rather than on the whole evidence set.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes the shortest route to a different interpretation is not adding more facts but moving one inference.
rituals.safety: Restrict the exercise to harmless puzzle material. If the exercise shifts into perfection pressure, stop the exercise; set the puzzle aside unfinished.

rituals.safety: For this round, choose information safe to forget. If the exercise shifts into compulsive rehearsal, finish there and release the items.

rituals.hook: Subtract what you actually observed from everything the thought is claiming.
rituals.rule: The remainder is inference, not automatically error.
rituals.play: Mentally list everything the thought says is true as set A. List only directly observed facts as set B. Remove every B item from A.
rituals.twist: Look at what remains and label it INFERENCE RESIDUE.
rituals.reveal: A large conclusion can contain a much smaller factual core plus a sizeable interpretive remainder.
rituals.mindBend: Separating inference from fact does not require disproving the inference; subtraction alone changes its status.
rituals.safety: Use a low-stakes mental game. Move on without rating yourself when perfection pressure shows up; do not continue the task.

rituals.hook: Move the problem out of your head one layer at a time without stacking a big story on a small fact.

rituals.twist: If a broad self-story has no supporting middle layer, it cannot be placed.
rituals.reveal: Overload can contain badly stacked abstraction rather than simply too many items.
rituals.mindBend: A large conclusion becomes unstable when it is balanced on a smaller fact than it can support.
rituals.safety: Use only neutral examples. If perfection pressure shows up, leave the round and move attention into a normal activity.

rituals.hook: Escape the current viewpoint with an L-shaped mental jump.

rituals.play: Choose two axes, such as TIME and PERSON. Move two steps on the first—today to one month from now—and one step on the second—you to a neutral observer.
rituals.twist: Ask the same question from that new coordinate without returning through the intermediate viewpoints.
rituals.reveal: A stuck thought can depend on remaining inside one local neighbourhood of perspective.
rituals.mindBend: Some viewpoints cannot be reached by a small straight shift; they require changing more than one dimension at once.
rituals.safety: Choose harmless puzzle material. If frustration turns into self-judgment, stop without rating your performance.

rituals.hook: Ask what would happen if you actively changed the suspected cause.
rituals.rule: An intervention changes the candidate cause rather than merely observing it.
rituals.play: Use a harmless example: coffee drinking and alertness rise together. Imagine actively setting coffee to zero while sleep and time of day stay the same. Ask what each causal story predicts.
rituals.twist: Do not treat correlation alone as the intervention result.

rituals.mindBend: INTERVENTION TEST reveals this: Two things moving together does not prove one caused the other.
rituals.safety: Use only a harmless, checkable claim. If real safety information is being dismissed, stop the thought experiment and verify the situation with an appropriate person or reliable source before continuing.

rituals.twist: Then apply the set rule: A includes all cases in B plus additional bank workers.
rituals.reveal: A vivid conjunction can feel more probable despite being mathematically a subset of the broader event.
rituals.mindBend: CONJUNCTION TRAP reveals this: Extra detail can make a story feel more believable while making it mathematically less probable.
rituals.safety: Keep this to low-stakes examples. If real safety facts start being discounted, end the exercise and seek appropriate real-world verification or professional assessment rather than reasoning past those facts.

rituals.twist: Keep barrier in place for the round.
rituals.reveal: The target action requires an extra step.
rituals.mindBend: One practical barrier between an urge and its target behaviour creates friction exactly where execution would begin.
rituals.safety: Use only a non-dangerous action urge. When greater access to harmful means becomes noticeable, stop and go to a safer place.

rituals.hook: Compress repeated mental runs into a tiny code.
rituals.rule: Consecutive repeats become one item plus a count.
rituals.play: Watch the thought for repeated operations such as CHECK, WHY, REPLAY, PREDICT. When the same operation repeats, code it as 3×CHECK or 4×WHY instead of following every copy.
rituals.twist: Reconstruct the original loop from the code and notice how much of its apparent length came from duplication.
rituals.reveal: A long rumination episode can contain very little unique cognitive content.
rituals.mindBend: Compression exposes the difference between how long a loop lasts and how much information it contains.
rituals.safety: Keep this to a low-stakes mental game for one pass. When self-judgment from frustration develops, leave the exercise; switch to an ordinary activity.

rituals.hook: Anchor to something outside your interpretation.

rituals.play: Read one stable external fact aloud or silently—such as a device clock, room sign, address, date display or printed label—and recheck the exact same fact once.
rituals.twist: If you still feel unable to verify what is happening, involve another person or professional support.
rituals.reveal: One present fact is anchored to an external source that can be checked again.

rituals.safety: This is a shared-reality aid, not proof that everything is fine; if frightening uncertainty persists, show the same external information to a trusted person or clinician instead of checking it alone repeatedly.

NEXT

WHY THIS MATTERS
Isolation risk decreases through visibility and contact.

REMEMBER
Remaining visible and connected during acute risk changes the conditions around dangerous action.
